name: Hydrochloric Acid
storageInstructions: Store in a cool, well-ventilated area in corrosion-resistant containers.
facts: Hydrochloric acid is produced naturally in the human stomach to aid digestion.
It was historically known as muriatic acid.

commonReactions.description: Reaction with zinc producing hydrogen gas

name: Sulfuric Acid
storageInstructions: Store in tightly closed containers in a cool, dry, well-ventilated area away from metals.
facts: Sulfuric acid is the most widely produced chemical in the world.
It is sometimes called the 'king of chemicals'.

name: Nitric Acid
storageInstructions: Store in a cool, dark place away from organic materials and reducing agents.
facts: Nitric acid can dissolve most metals except gold and platinum.
Mixed with hydrochloric acid, it forms aqua regia which can dissolve gold.

name: Acetic Acid
storageInstructions: Store in tightly sealed containers away from heat and open flames.
facts: Vinegar is essentially a dilute solution of acetic acid (about 5%).
Pure acetic acid is called glacial acetic acid because it freezes at 16.6°C.

name: Phosphoric Acid
storageInstructions: Store in corrosion-resistant containers in a cool, dry area.
facts: Phosphoric acid is used in many soft drinks to provide a tangy taste.
It is a triprotic acid, meaning it can donate three protons.

name: Hydrofluoric Acid
storageInstructions: Store in polyethylene or Teflon containers. NEVER use glass. Handle with extreme caution.
facts: HF can dissolve glass, which is why it must be stored in plastic containers.
Despite being a weak acid, HF is one of the most dangerous acids due to its ability to penetrate skin.

name: Hydrobromic Acid
storageInstructions: Store in tightly closed containers in a well-ventilated area.
facts: Hydrobromic acid is one of the strongest mineral acids.

name: Carbonic Acid
storageInstructions: Exists only in solution; store carbonated solutions sealed.
facts: Carbonic acid forms when CO₂ dissolves in water and is responsible for the fizz in soda.
It plays a crucial role in regulating blood pH in the human body.

commonReactions.description: Decomposition into water and carbon dioxide

name: Perchloric Acid
storageInstructions: Store away from organic materials and reducing agents in a cool location.
facts: Perchloric acid is the strongest of the common mineral acids.
Concentrated perchloric acid is a powerful oxidizer and can cause explosions.

name: Citric Acid
storageInstructions: Store in a dry, cool area in sealed containers.
facts: Citric acid is naturally found in citrus fruits like lemons and oranges.
It is one of the most widely used food additives worldwide.

name: Sodium Hydroxide
storageInstructions: Store in tightly sealed containers away from acids and moisture. Use corrosion-resistant storage.
facts: Sodium hydroxide is commonly known as lye or caustic soda.
It is used in the process of making pretzels to give them their distinctive brown crust.

name: Potassium Hydroxide
storageInstructions: Store in airtight containers away from acids and moisture.
facts: Potassium hydroxide is used to make soft or liquid soaps, unlike NaOH which makes hard bar soaps.

name: Calcium Hydroxide
storageInstructions: Store in sealed containers in a dry place. Absorbs CO₂ from air.
facts: Calcium hydroxide solution (limewater) turns milky when CO₂ is bubbled through it.
It is commonly known as slaked lime.

name: Ammonia
storageInstructions: Store in well-ventilated areas in pressurized containers away from acids.
facts: Ammonia is produced on a massive scale by the Haber-Bosch process.
It has a distinctive smell that is commonly associated with cleaning products.

commonReactions.description: Acts as a weak base in water

name: Magnesium Hydroxide
hazards: May cause diarrhea in large doses
storageInstructions: Store in sealed containers in a cool, dry place.
facts: Magnesium hydroxide is the active ingredient in Milk of Magnesia.
It neutralizes stomach acid without producing CO₂ gas.

name: Barium Hydroxide
storageInstructions: Store in tightly closed containers away from CO₂ and moisture.
facts: Barium hydroxide reacting with ammonium thiocyanate is a famous endothermic reaction that can freeze water.

commonReactions.description: Double replacement forming insoluble barium sulfate

name: Sodium Chloride
storageInstructions: Store in a dry place in sealed containers.
facts: Sodium chloride makes up about 3.5% of the world's oceans.
Humans need about 500 mg of sodium per day to maintain vital functions.

name: Potassium Bromide
hazards: Harmful if swallowed in large amounts
storageInstructions: Store in a cool, dry place.
facts: Potassium bromide was used as an anti-seizure medication in the 19th century and is still used in veterinary medicine.

name: Calcium Carbonate
solubility: Insoluble in water, soluble in acids
hazards: Dust may irritate eyes and respiratory tract
storageInstructions: Store in a dry place away from acids.
facts: Calcium carbonate is the main component of limestone, marble, and chalk.
Eggshells are about 95% calcium carbonate.

name: Copper(II) Sulfate
storageInstructions: Store in a dry area away from metals and moisture.
facts: Anhydrous copper sulfate is white and turns blue when water is added — a classic test for water.
The beautiful blue crystals of copper sulfate pentahydrate are a popular chemistry demonstration.

name: Silver Nitrate
storageInstructions: Store in dark bottles away from light and organic materials.
facts: Silver nitrate stains skin and clothing black due to the photoreduction of silver ions.
It has been used medicinally since the Middle Ages.

commonReactions.description: Pale yellow precipitate of silver bromide

name: Sodium Carbonate
storageInstructions: Store in a dry place in sealed containers.
facts: Sodium carbonate is commonly known as washing soda or soda ash.
Ancient Egyptians used natron (a natural form of sodium carbonate) for mummification.

name: Potassium Permanganate
storageInstructions: Store away from combustible materials, reducing agents, and acids.
facts: A single crystal of KMnO₄ dropped in water creates a beautiful purple trail due to diffusion.
It is used as a self-indicator in titrations because its purple color disappears at the endpoint.

name: Sodium Bicarbonate
storageInstructions: Store in a cool, dry place.
facts: Baking soda (sodium bicarbonate) reacting with vinegar is one of the most classic chemistry demonstrations.
It is used in fire extinguishers because it releases CO₂ when heated.

name: Ammonium Chloride
storageInstructions: Store in sealed containers in a cool, dry place.
facts: Ammonium chloride is used in some types of licorice candy in Nordic countries.
It sublimes (goes directly from solid to gas) when heated.

commonReactions.description: Releases ammonia gas when heated with a base

name: Iron
storageInstructions: Store in a dry place to prevent rusting.
facts: Iron is the most used metal in the world.
The Earth's core is primarily composed of iron and nickel.
Iron is essential for hemoglobin in blood.

commonReactions.description: Iron displaces copper from copper sulfate

name: Copper
storageInstructions: Store in a dry area. No special requirements.
facts: Copper was the first metal to be worked by humans around 10,000 years ago.
The Statue of Liberty is covered in copper, which has turned green due to oxidation (patina).

name: Zinc
storageInstructions: Store zinc dust away from heat and moisture in sealed containers.
facts: Zinc is essential for the human body and is found in every cell.
Galvanization with zinc protects iron from rusting through sacrificial protection.

name: Aluminum
storageInstructions: Store in a dry place. Keep aluminum powder away from ignition sources.
facts: Aluminum is the most abundant metal in the Earth's crust.
Before the Hall-Héroult process was invented, aluminum was more valuable than gold.

name: Sodium
storageInstructions: Store under mineral oil or kerosene. Keep away from water and moisture at all times.
facts: Sodium is soft enough to cut with a knife.
When thrown into water, sodium reacts so violently it can catch fire or explode.

name: Potassium
storageInstructions: Store under mineral oil. Handle with extreme caution, away from water.
facts: Potassium reacts even more violently with water than sodium.
It produces a characteristic violet/lilac flame color.

name: Magnesium
solubility: Reacts slowly with water (rapidly with steam)
storageInstructions: Store in a dry place away from water and oxidizers. Keep ribbon/powder away from flames.
facts: Magnesium burns with such an intense white light that it was once used in camera flash bulbs.
It cannot be extinguished with water — doing so makes it burn more violently.

name: Calcium
storageInstructions: Store in airtight containers under argon or mineral oil.
facts: Calcium is the fifth most abundant element in the Earth's crust.
The human body contains about 1 kg of calcium, mostly in bones and teeth.

name: Silver
storageInstructions: Store in a dry, tarnish-resistant environment.
facts: Silver has the highest electrical conductivity of any element.
Silver ions have natural antibacterial properties.

name: Gold
solubility: Insoluble in water and most acids
storageInstructions: Store securely. No special chemical storage requirements.
facts: Gold is so malleable that a single ounce can be beaten into a 300 sq ft sheet.
All the gold ever mined would fit in about 3.5 Olympic swimming pools.
Gold can only be dissolved by aqua regia (HNO₃ + HCl mixture).

name: Lead
storageInstructions: Handle with care. Wash hands after handling. Store away from acids.
facts: Lead poisoning was a major issue in ancient Rome, where lead pipes were used for plumbing.
The word 'plumbing' comes from 'plumbum', the Latin word for lead.

name: Tin
storageInstructions: Store in a cool, dry place.
facts: Tin is one of the earliest metals known to humans, used in bronze alloys since 3000 BCE.
When tin is bent, it produces a crackling sound known as the 'tin cry'.

name: Oxygen
storageInstructions: Store compressed oxygen cylinders upright, secured, and away from flammable materials.
facts: Oxygen makes up about 21% of Earth's atmosphere.
Liquid oxygen is pale blue in color.
Oxygen is the third most abundant element in the universe.

name: Nitrogen
storageInstructions: Store compressed nitrogen in well-ventilated areas. Handle liquid nitrogen with cryogenic gloves.
facts: Nitrogen makes up about 78% of Earth's atmosphere.
Despite being abundant in air, nitrogen gas is quite unreactive due to its strong triple bond.

commonReactions.description: Synthesis of ammonia under high pressure and temperature

name: Chlorine
hazards: Was used as chemical weapon in WWI
storageInstructions: Store in well-ventilated areas in approved cylinders. Use in fume hood only.
facts: Chlorine was used as a chemical weapon in World War I.
It is essential for water purification and saves millions of lives from waterborne diseases.

commonReactions.description: Reaction with sodium hydroxide forming bleach

name: Sulfur
odor: Odorless (elemental); compounds smell like rotten eggs
storageInstructions: Store in a cool, dry place away from oxidizers and heat.
facts: Sulfur was known as 'brimstone' in ancient times.
It burns with a blue flame producing sulfur dioxide.

name: Phosphorus (White)
solubility: Insoluble in water; soluble in carbon disulfide
storageInstructions: Must be stored under water to prevent spontaneous ignition.
facts: White phosphorus glows in the dark (phosphorescence is named after it).
It must be kept under water because it ignites spontaneously in air.

name: Carbon
storageInstructions: Store in a dry place.
facts: Carbon is the basis of all known life on Earth.
Diamond and graphite are both pure carbon but have completely different properties.
A pencil 'lead' is actually graphite (carbon), not lead.

name: Hydrogen
storageInstructions: Store in approved cylinders in well-ventilated areas away from ignition sources.
facts: Hydrogen is the most abundant element in the universe.
The sun is primarily composed of hydrogen undergoing nuclear fusion.
Hydrogen burns with a nearly invisible pale blue flame.

name: Bromine
storageInstructions: Store in glass containers with Teflon-lined caps in a fume hood.
facts: Bromine is one of only two elements that are liquid at room temperature (the other is mercury).
Its name comes from the Greek 'bromos' meaning 'stench'.

name: Iodine
solubility: Slightly soluble in water; soluble in KI solution
storageInstructions: Store in dark, sealed containers in a cool place.
facts: Iodine sublimes easily — it goes directly from solid to a beautiful violet vapor.
Iodine turns starch blue-black, which is one of the most well-known chemical tests.

name: Methane
storageInstructions: Store in approved gas cylinders away from ignition sources in ventilated areas.
facts: Methane is the simplest hydrocarbon.
Cows produce significant amounts of methane through digestion.
It is about 80 times more potent as a greenhouse gas than CO₂ over 20 years.

name: Ethanol
storageInstructions: Store in tightly sealed containers away from heat and ignition sources.
facts: Ethanol is the type of alcohol found in alcoholic beverages.
It has been produced by fermentation for at least 9,000 years.
Ethanol burns with a nearly invisible blue flame.

name: Glucose
storageInstructions: Store in a cool, dry place in sealed containers.
facts: Glucose is the primary source of energy for the body's cells.
It is the most abundant monosaccharide in nature.
Photosynthesis in plants produces glucose from CO₂ and water.

name: Benzene
solubility: Slightly soluble in water; miscible with organic solvents
storageInstructions: Store in a well-ventilated area away from heat. Use in fume hoods.
facts: Benzene's ring structure was famously proposed by August Kekulé, who allegedly dreamed of a snake biting its own tail.
Despite its sweet smell, benzene is a known carcinogen and its use as a solvent has been largely discontinued.

name: Acetone
storageInstructions: Store away from heat, sparks, and open flames in a well-ventilated area.
facts: Acetone is produced naturally in the human body during fat metabolism.
It is the simplest ketone.

name: Formaldehyde
solubility: Very soluble in water (formalin is 37% solution)
storageInstructions: Store in a cool, ventilated area. Use in fume hoods.
facts: Formaldehyde is the simplest aldehyde.
Formalin (aqueous formaldehyde) is used to preserve biological specimens.

name: Urea
storageInstructions: Store in a cool, dry place.
facts: Urea was the first organic compound synthesized from inorganic materials by Friedrich Wöhler in 1828.
This disproved the theory of vitalism (that organic compounds could only come from living organisms).

name: Carbon Dioxide
storageInstructions: Store compressed CO₂ cylinders in ventilated areas.
facts: Dry ice is solid CO₂ at -78.5°C.
Plants absorb CO₂ during photosynthesis.
CO₂ concentration in Earth's atmosphere has risen from 280 ppm (pre-industrial) to over 420 ppm.

name: Carbon Monoxide
storageInstructions: Store in approved cylinders with CO detectors. Handle with extreme care.
facts: Carbon monoxide is called the 'silent killer' because it is odorless and tasteless.
It binds to hemoglobin about 200 times more strongly than oxygen does.

commonReactions.description: Reduction of iron ore in blast furnace

name: Sulfur Dioxide
storageInstructions: Store in approved cylinders in well-ventilated areas.
facts: SO₂ is a major contributor to acid rain.
Volcanic eruptions release massive amounts of SO₂.
It has been used as a food preservative since Roman times.

name: Nitrogen Dioxide
storageInstructions: Store in approved cylinders in well-ventilated areas away from combustibles.
facts: NO₂ gives smog its brown color.
It is responsible for the brown fumes seen when metals dissolve in nitric acid.

name: Hydrogen Sulfide
solubility: Slightly soluble in water (forms weak acid)
hazards: Deadens sense of smell at high concentrations
storageInstructions: Store in approved cylinders in well-ventilated areas. Use H₂S detectors.
facts: H₂S is the chemical responsible for the smell of rotten eggs.
At high concentrations, it paralyzes the olfactory nerve, making it undetectable by smell — extremely dangerous.

name: Ozone
storageInstructions: Must be generated on-site; cannot be stored effectively.
facts: The ozone layer in the stratosphere protects Earth from UV radiation.
Ozone at ground level is a pollutant and component of smog.
Its name comes from the Greek 'ozein' meaning 'to smell'.

name: Nitrous Oxide
storageInstructions: Store cylinders in ventilated areas away from combustibles.
facts: Nitrous oxide is commonly known as 'laughing gas' due to the euphoric effects when inhaled.
It is about 300 times more potent as a greenhouse gas than CO₂.

name: Hydrogen Peroxide
storageInstructions: Store in original container in a cool, dark place. Never mix with organic materials.
facts: Bombardier beetles use hydrogen peroxide in their defense mechanism, creating a boiling hot chemical spray.
Concentrated H₂O₂ (90%+) was used as rocket fuel (e.g., in V-2 rockets).

name: Potassium Dichromate
storageInstructions: Store away from combustibles and reducing agents. Use appropriate PPE.
facts: K₂Cr₂O₇ was traditionally used in breathalyzer tests — it changes from orange to green in the presence of ethanol.
Chromium(VI) compounds are known carcinogens.

name: Manganese Dioxide
storageInstructions: Store in a cool, dry place away from combustible materials.
facts: MnO₂ is the natural mineral pyrolusite.
It is the most commonly used catalyst for decomposing hydrogen peroxide in chemistry labs.

name: Potassium Nitrate
storageInstructions: Store away from combustible materials and reducing agents.
facts: Potassium nitrate is one of the three components of traditional gunpowder (with charcoal and sulfur).
It is historically known as 'saltpeter'.

name: Sodium Thiosulfate
storageInstructions: Store in a cool, dry place.
facts: Sodium thiosulfate is used as 'hypo' in photography to fix photographic images.
It is used in the famous 'iodine clock reaction' demonstration.

commonReactions.equation: Na₂S₂O₃ + HCl → NaCl + S↓ + SO₂ + H₂O

name: Iron(II) Sulfate
storageInstructions: Store in sealed containers away from moisture and oxidizers.
facts: Iron(II) sulfate heptahydrate is historically known as green vitriol.
It is used as an iron supplement to treat anemia.

name: Oxalic Acid
storageInstructions: Store in a cool, dry place in sealed containers.
facts: Oxalic acid is found naturally in many plants, including rhubarb and spinach.
It is used to remove rust stains from fabric.

name: Sodium Sulfite
hazards: May cause allergic reactions in sensitive individuals
storageInstructions: Store in sealed containers away from acids and oxidizers.
facts: Sodium sulfite is used in food preservation to prevent browning.
Some people are sensitive to sulfites and may have allergic reactions.

name: Water
storageInstructions: No special storage requirements.
facts: Water is the only substance that naturally exists in all three states of matter on Earth.
Water molecules are bent at an angle of about 104.5°.
About 71% of Earth's surface is covered in water.

name: Potassium Iodide
storageInstructions: Store in a dark, cool, dry place in sealed containers.
facts: KI is added to table salt to prevent iodine deficiency disorders.
KI tablets are distributed near nuclear facilities as a thyroid-protective measure during radiation emergencies.

name: Lead(II) Nitrate
storageInstructions: Store in sealed containers. Handle with PPE. Dispose as hazardous waste.
facts: The reaction of lead nitrate with potassium iodide produces a beautiful 'golden rain' of yellow lead iodide crystals when done in a warm solution.

name: Calcium Chloride
storageInstructions: Store in sealed containers in a dry place. Absorbs moisture readily.
facts: Calcium chloride dissolving in water is noticeably exothermic — the solution gets warm.
It can lower the freezing point of water to about -52°C, making it effective for de-icing.

name: Sodium Sulfate
storageInstructions: Store in a cool, dry place.
facts: Sodium sulfate decahydrate (Glauber's salt) was one of the first 'miracle drugs' in 17th century medicine, used as a laxative.

commonReactions.description: White precipitate of barium sulfate (sulfate test)

name: Barium Chloride
storageInstructions: Store in sealed containers. Handle with care.
facts: Barium chloride is the standard reagent for testing for sulfate ions in solution — a white precipitate of BaSO₄ confirms their presence.

name: Methanol
hazards: Can cause blindness and death if ingested
storageInstructions: Store in tightly closed containers away from heat and ignition sources.
facts: Methanol is also called wood alcohol because it was originally obtained by distilling wood.
Drinking even small amounts of methanol can cause permanent blindness.

name: Ethylene Glycol
hazards: Sweet taste makes accidental ingestion a risk
storageInstructions: Store securely away from children and pets due to its sweet taste and toxicity.
facts: Ethylene glycol tastes sweet, which unfortunately makes it attractive to children and pets — it is highly toxic.
It is the main component of most automobile antifreeze products.

name: Sodium Hypochlorite
hazards: Toxic fumes when mixed with acids
storageInstructions: Store in a cool, dark place. NEVER mix with acids or ammonia.
facts: Household bleach is typically a 3-6% solution of sodium hypochlorite.
Mixing bleach with ammonia produces toxic chloramine gas — a common household poisoning source.

commonReactions.description: Produces toxic chlorine gas with acid — DANGEROUS

name: Calcium Oxide
storageInstructions: Store in airtight containers away from moisture.
facts: Calcium oxide is commonly known as quicklime.
When water is added to quicklime, it produces so much heat that it can boil the water.

commonReactions.description: Slaking — produces slaked lime with intense heat

name: Sodium Acetate
storageInstructions: Store in a cool, dry place.
facts: Sodium acetate trihydrate is used in reusable hand warmers — it can form a supersaturated solution that releases heat when crystallized.
Hot ice demonstrations use supersaturated sodium acetate solutions.

name: Zinc Sulfate
storageInstructions: Store in a dry place in sealed containers.
facts: Zinc sulfate is commonly used as a dietary zinc supplement.
It is also known as white vitriol.

name: Iron(III) Chloride
storageInstructions: Store in tightly sealed containers. Absorbs moisture.
facts: Iron(III) chloride turns purple/violet with phenol — this is a classic test for phenolic compounds.

commonReactions.description: Rusty brown precipitate of iron(III) hydroxide

name: Propane
storageInstructions: Store in approved pressurized cylinders away from heat and ignition sources.
facts: Propane is one of the main components of LPG (liquefied petroleum gas).
It is heavier than air, so leaks can accumulate in low-lying areas.

name: Sucrose
storageInstructions: Store in a cool, dry place.
facts: When concentrated sulfuric acid is added to sucrose, it dehydrates the sugar to pure carbon in a dramatic 'sugar snake' demonstration.
Sucrose is composed of one glucose and one fructose molecule linked together.

name: Lithium
storageInstructions: Store under mineral oil away from water and moisture.
facts: Lithium is the lightest metal and the least dense solid element.
It floats on water while reacting with it.
Lithium compounds are used to treat bipolar disorder.

commonReactions.description: Gentle reaction with water (less violent than Na or K)

name: Strontium Chloride
storageInstructions: Store in a cool, dry place.
facts: Strontium compounds produce a brilliant red color in fireworks and flares.
Strontium is named after the Scottish village of Strontian where the mineral strontianite was discovered.

name: Copper(II) Chloride
storageInstructions: Store in sealed containers away from metals.
facts: Copper(II) chloride produces a beautiful blue-green flame color.
It is used as a catalyst in several industrial chemical processes.
